1.pericope_label: See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh

schools.summary: Calvin reads the title as a remedy for the anxiety and unbelief the prophet had shown: he was furnished with supreme authority, whereby he should cast down the tyrant's pride. Yet God took nothing from himself to transfer it, since he so communicates what is peculiar to himself as to remain himself in his completeness; when he seems to resign a part of his glory to his ministers, he only teaches that the efficacy of his Spirit will be joined with their labours, that these may not be fruitless. The name of prophet Calvin uses for an interpreter, since that office proceeds from God alone; and because God delivered through the one to the other what he wished said, Aaron is made subject to his brother as if to God himself — a subjection made clearer in the verse following, where the power granted is circumscribed. Gill notes that the whole answer meets an objection taken from the prophet's own meanness and the majesty of Pharaoh.

Henry takes the title as an office, and marks its limits carefully. God clothes Moses with great power in making him a god to Pharaoh, that is, his representative in this affair, as magistrates are called gods because they are God's vicegerents; he was authorised to act in God's name, endued with power to do what is above the ordinary course of nature, and invested with authority to demand obedience of a sovereign prince. But it was a made deity, not one held essentially by nature, and none but by commission; and it reached only to Pharaoh, whereas the living and true God is God to all the world. Henry finds it an instance of condescension that when God treats with men he treats by men, whose terror shall not make us afraid. Aaron is named as an assistant, not a man of uncircumcised lips but a notable spokesman, who shall speak from him to Pharaoh as prophets do from God to men.

Wesley follows Henry almost word for word on the made deity and the commission, and on the prophet who speaks from him as prophets speak from God. Clarke says the same in a sentence — at his word every plague should come and at his command each be removed — and sets out the chapter's argument: the dignified mission of the two, the prediction that the king's heart should be hardened that God might multiply his signs, the rod turned into a serpent and imitated by the magicians, the threat at the river, the waters turned to blood, and the plague enduring seven days.

Ellicott takes the whole as God's answer to the objection about uncircumcised lips, probably following it at once, and states its force sharply: Moses is not called on to speak but to act. In action he will be as a god, powerful, wonder-working, irresistible, while his brother, who is eloquent, must do the speaking; and prophet he would render spokesman, the declarer of another's mind, which is the primary sense. Keil observes that the word rendered armies is used of Israel leaving Egypt equipped and organised by tribes, to contend for the cause of the Lord and fight his battles — in which respect they are called the hosts of Jehovah.

supreme authority given without any diminution of God, whose Spirit works with the minister
not a call to speak but to act — in action powerful, wonder-working, irresistible

outliers.note: reads the military sense of the word for armies, Israel leaving Egypt organised by tribes to fight the battles of the Lord

themes: a god to Pharaoh and a prophet to Moses
whether the title is essential or by commission
Israel as the armies of the Lord

3.pericope_label: I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and multiply my signs

schools.summary: Calvin allows that the expression is harsh and that many take pains to soften it, but refuses the softening. He renders the clauses adversatively — I indeed will harden his heart, but I will multiply my signs — as though the hardness were no obstacle, the wonders sufficing to overcome it; and he does not reject the alternative that God willed the resistance so that the deliverance might be more conspicuous. What he will not allow is a bare permission: they are but poor speculators who refer it there, since in blinding minds God inflicts deserved punishment, executing a judgment he knows to be just and delivering to Satan those who deserve such blindness. The blame still rests with the men, who with a willfulness like madness rush into sin; and those who make God the author of evil confuse two things, for the hardness of heart is the sin of man, but the hardening of the heart is the judgment of God. Calvin hears a species of irony in the promise that Egypt shall know the name, since the acknowledgment is extorted from the unwilling, who oppose an iron obstinacy to every threatening until violence forces them into alarm — like drunkards roused from their stupor who would gladly sleep on, yet must bear the pains of their intemperance. Gill takes the announcement of the refusal pastorally, as told beforehand lest the brothers be discouraged and think their labour vain.

Clarke gives the softer construction without argument: God will permit the stubbornness still to remain, that he may have the greater opportunity to multiply his wonders in the land. The same permitted opposition he reads as mercy to Egypt, that the departure might be so signal that the Almighty should appear all-sufficient.

Ellicott refers the hardening back to the fourth chapter and adds a distinction among the terms: signs were miracles done as credentials, proving a mission; wonders were miracles generally; a third word, also rendered wonders, denotes those wrought in the way of punishment, elsewhere called judgments. On the syntax of the next verse he is careful — the Hebrew is not that Pharaoh shall not hearken so that God may lay on his hand, but that he will not hearken, and God will lay it on, no relation of effect and cause being asserted between two co-ordinate clauses; and the armies and the people stand in apposition, the second explaining the first. On the stated end he presses hard: to know the name is to know that its bearer answers to it, the only really existing God, the so-called gods of Egypt being vapour, smoke, nothingness. Egypt was then the greatest monarchy in the world and at the height of her glory, and among existing polytheisms hers was the most famous, so that to discredit her gods was to discredit polytheism generally. Keil marks the shape of the section, which opens with a sign attesting the commission and closes with the last blow announced, the nine plagues at its centre.

themes: I will harden Pharaoh’s heart
signs, wonders and judgments distinguished

6.pericope_label: Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded them

schools.summary: Calvin insists it is not for boasting that the historian records his own compliance: having confessed his earlier hesitation, he now relates that the two were in better courage for their office, bringing no talent or dexterity of their own but simply obeying — and as we may attempt nothing except what God prescribes, so we ought without objection to pursue whatever he commands. The ages that follow he takes as an amplification. It was no common case that two octogenarians should engage actively in so difficult a charge, and he will not join those who think their years merely enhanced their dignity; the point is rather that, excluding all human means, the glory might be celebrated of a God who performed so mighty a work by men failing and decrepit, who might themselves have been timid and troubled the people. On the demand for a sign Calvin finds a usual mark of unbelief: they ask for proofs of power which they may still discredit, not professedly scorning God but urged by secret impiety to seek subterfuges, and when the sign is given they seek deeper lurking places. Gill adds that afterwards the brothers never objected to any errand but set about it cheerfully, and takes the tally of years as marking how long the affliction had run.

Henry observes that the first approach produced only the instructions, and that now the credentials are called for. It is taken for granted that the king will challenge the demandants to work something evidently above the power of nature, and so prove a commission from the God of nature — yet he asks with no desire to be convinced, hoping nothing will be wrought and that he may then have colour for his infidelity. Henry follows the contest through: the staff that was to signal every later wonder is itself made the subject of one, to put a reputation upon it; serpents are dreadful creatures, and the sight might have softened the king into fear, so that though no plague it amounted to the threat of one. The imitation drained the conviction away, whether the rods became serpents by permitted delusion or by evil angels substituting; but the swallowing settled it, great truth prevailing.

Clarke does the arithmetic of the ages — forty years before Midian and forty in Midian, the elder brother three years the senior — and defines the word for a miracle as an effect opposed to the laws of nature, or such as her powers are inadequate to produce, adding that it has ever been the sense of mankind that one sent on so singular an errand can give supernatural evidence of it. Wesley draws the contrast with Joseph, who was to be only a servant to Pharaoh and was preferred at thirty, whereas the man who was to be a god to Pharaoh waited till eighty: fit that such honour be long awaited and such service long prepared for.

Ellicott marks the turn in the narrative: from here the resistance ceases, the leader subdues his own will and earns the praise of being faithful as a servant in all God's house, while his brother's obedience continues until Sinai, where it failed before the frenzy of the people. On the ages he observes that the air of Egypt, and still more of the desert, favoured long life, the monuments showing officials employed past a hundred. He suspects the king had heard of the signs wrought before Israel and was curious to witness one, as Herod was later, or expected his own magicians to show greater and so dismiss the brothers as impostors. Keil argues that the rod, called Aaron's here because entrusted to him, is the same wondrous staff of the fourth chapter, since the one held over the waters afterwards must be the one turned into a serpent now.

as chronology, forty years before Midian and forty in Midian, the elder brother three years the senior
as a contrast with Joseph, dignified at thirty as a servant where this man waited till eighty as a god to Pharaoh

outliers.note: notes from the Egyptian monuments that officials were often actively employed past a hundred, the air of Egypt and the desert favouring longevity

themes: Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded
the ages of the two brothers
shew a miracle for you

10.pericope_label: Aaron cast down his rod, and it became a serpent

schools.summary: Calvin observes that even men conscious of their vocation and armed with power for wonders would never have dared approach so fierce a tyrant, had not the inward inspiration of the Spirit steeled them to persevere, raising them by faith above everything lofty on earth. On whether the change of the staff was substantial he is confident that it was: there is no more difficulty with God in changing the forms of things than in creating heaven and earth out of nothing, and since this ran contrary to nature's course we must judge of it as of the pillar of salt, save that the staff soon returned to its first form. Of the rival rods he is less sure, allowing that the king's eyes may have been deceived, yet finding nothing absurd in saying such liberty was conceded — not to create one body out of another, but to set forth God's work as their own — since the potency of error far surpasses our comprehension, and is given, as Paul says, that those who will not obey the truth should believe a lie. He remarks the courtesy of the title borne by the court's men: they are honourably called wise though inventors of deceit, for though astronomy flourished among them their degenerate science was vanity, as Satan conceals falsehood under specious titles. Gill has the brothers entering the palace boldly, clothed with authority and assured of success, and calls the magicians jugglers who cast a mist before people's eyes.

Clarke is exercised by the noun for the creature: the word here is not the one used at the burning bush but the term elsewhere rendered whale, dragon or sea-monster, used of some very large creature, aquatic or amphibious, and some have thought the crocodile is meant — the objection that a staff and a common snake are of comparable size he sets aside, since a miracle was being wrought. He renders the three classes of the court's men as men of learning, revealers of hidden things and decipherers of abstruse writings, and traces the word for their enchantments to a root meaning to burn, supposing rites of lustral fires, fumigations and aromatic drugs by which assistant spirits were evoked. Against the theory of mere conjuring he argues that if the rods became serpents after being thrown down, dexterity had nothing to do with it, the rods being out of their hands, and no nimbleness accounts for one devouring the rest. Wesley compresses the closing clause to permission.

Ellicott gives the same three classes as wise men, mutterers of charms, and scribes or writers of charms, and describes how widely the art was practised: a large part of the Ritual of the Dead is charms for the soul to utter in Hades to pass the monsters it would meet, and other works survive as mere collections of magical receipts. He notes the Jewish tradition, taken up by Paul, which named two of them, one famous enough to be named by Pliny and Apuleius. On the contest itself he inclines to think the men merely knew secrets of nature not generally known and were trained in sleight of hand, and suggests the trick familiar to Egyptian serpent-charmers in every age, by which a charmed reptile is made to look like a stick and then disenchanted. On the closing clause he insists the verb is intransitive and the received rendering a mistranslation — Pharaoh's heart hardened itself — since a final penal hardening requires that in the earlier stages the man be left to himself.

probably sleight of hand or the serpent-charmer’s trick, the men knowing only secrets of nature not generally known
the eyes of the wicked were likely deceived, God conceding liberty for them to set forth his work as their own

themes: the rod that became a serpent

14.pericope_label: Pharaoh's heart is hardened, he refuseth to let the people go

schools.summary: Calvin sees in this single reprobate a picture of human pride wherever it is not controlled by tractableness, and warns the faithful against provoking a like vengeance, since the same Being who hardened him avenges impiety constantly, smiting his enemies with confusion and rendering them as furious as they are senseless. He also hears encouragement in the announcement: told the heart was hardened, the messenger might waver unless hope of victory were shown him, and so God arms his servant afresh, as if to say the beast must be worn down though it could not be broken. He adds, though some will think it far-fetched, that the ten plagues answer to the ten precepts, the wicked smitten with as many strokes as God was about to give commandments. Gill renders the word for the hardening as heavy, dull and stupid, so that the king cannot lift up his heart to obey.

Henry weighs the stroke under three heads. It was dreadful: nothing is more common than water, so kindly has Providence ordered that what is needful to life be cheap and everywhere had, yet now Egypt must drink blood or die of thirst, and the fish that were much of their food died, the land made loathsome by the stench. It was righteous, for the river was their idol, served above the Creator; God turned into blood what they had turned into a god — that creature which we idolize he justly removes or embitters, making a scourge of what we set up as a competitor — and they had stained that water with the blood of Hebrew children, and now had blood to drink. And it was significant, since Egypt so depended on the river that smiting it warned of ruin running through every product of the land until it reached the firstborn, the red stream a direful omen of the Red Sea. Henry also reasons out the meeting-place: the messenger might not be admitted to the presence-chamber where ambassadors had audience, and so is sent to the bank, where God foresaw the king would come — for thus all people will walk, every one in the name of his god. He closes with a comparison: one of the first miracles here was water turned to blood, one of the first wrought by our Lord water turned to wine.

Clarke reads the same term as become heavy or stupid — no conviction is received, for all the clearness of the light shining on him — and adds what we know of prejudice: where men are set on a predetermined plan, arguments, demonstrations and even miracles are lost upon them, as with the obstinate opponents of the apostles.

Keil insists that neither the hour nor the place of the next meeting is incidental. The king goes out in the morning to the river, not for an airing or to see how high the water had risen, but beyond doubt to present his daily worship to the Nile, which Egypt honoured as supreme deity; and at that moment God's will concerning Israel is declared to him.

debates.question: Why is the summons delivered at the river's bank rather than at court?

positions.position: because the king went out to present his daily worship to the Nile, and the will of God met him at that moment
because the messenger might not be admitted to the presence-chamber where ambassadors had audience

outliers.note: proposes that the ten plagues answer in number to the ten precepts, the wicked smitten with as many strokes as God was about to give commandments

themes: Pharaoh’s heart is heavy
the first plague as dreadful, righteous and significant
the morning worship of the Nile

15.pericope_label: Lo, he goeth out unto the water: the Egyptians shall lothe to drink

schools.summary: Gill notes the hour, the next morning, when the mind is most composed, fit to attend to what is suggested; and he takes the promised knowledge plainly, as coming by an instance of power and vengeance. On the death of the fish he gives the simple reason: their element was changed and they could live in no other.

Clarke thinks the king went out for bathing or some religious washing, and cites the report that nothing stood in greater honour among the Egyptians than their river; he passes on too the older Jewish supposition that the king was himself a magician, walking out each morning to prepare his rites. He marks this verse as the opening of the series and reproduces a chronology placing all ten plagues within one month, from blood on the eighteenth of the sixth month to the firstborn slain on the fifteenth of Abib, then sets his own caution against it: most of these dates are destitute of proof. On the threatened loathing he quotes at length, since nothing carries here without knowing how pleasant and wholesome that water was reckoned. One traveller reports it so delicious that one would not wish the heat less, nor be delivered from thirst; that the Turks found it so exquisite they ate salt to make themselves drink more; that Egyptians abroad spoke of nothing but the pleasure of drinking it at their return, preferring that to the sight of their families; and that it should rank among waters as champagne among wines. Its best quality was that it never incommoded, some drinking three buckets a day — and this of the river only, their well water being detestable, fountains a kind of prodigy, and rain out of the question. Another adds that whoever has not heard this will never have felt the energy of the threat: they shall loathe the water they preferred to all the waters of the world, and choose rather the wells they abhorred.

Ellicott offers the bathing too, recalling the princess who drew the infant from the reeds, or else some festival in the river's honour, of which the calendar held several; and he renders the place of waiting literally, the lip of the river. The message is to be delivered with name and title in full, for at the first application the king had professed not to know who Jehovah was; and the complaint that follows is not that he had not listened but that he had not obeyed. He notes how the smiting is claimed — the rod in my hand means in the hand of my servant, God representing himself as about to do what was in fact done by another, since he who acts through another acts himself. On the loss of the fish he supplies what Clarke does not: the river's natural discolorations, by red earth or minute organisms, harm the fish nothing and leave the water fit for use, but the fish were a large part of the people's subsistence, so that to lose them was severe, with implied contempt of their religion besides, three species at least being sacred. The stench he will not explain away by the river's occasional natural odour, too slight for what is meant here.

19.pericope_label: All the waters that were in the river were turned to blood

schools.summary: Calvin asks why this stroke came first, answering from what the river was to Egypt. Great wealth, defence and convenience arose from it: the fisheries, the fertility of a country watered by its overflow — a thing injurious elsewhere — the navigation, and the fortification it made for much of the kingdom; so to cast them down from their chief dependence its waters are turned to blood. Since water is one of the two elements of which our life consists, to take away one part of life was the shortest way of humbling them, had they not been wholly intractable. God might by a single breath have dried up every source and overwhelmed them with drought, but that would have been thought chance or nature, a less apparent prodigy, and would have shut up the way for the rest. The listing of streams and ponds follows because the river was so diffused, by art and nature, that scarcely any country is so supplied — as if to say the store shall avail nothing, for they shall thirst as though the Nile were dry. Calvin also observes that the counsellors saw it, which argues the same infatuation through the court, and that it marked the nation's reprobation that none of that multitude laboured to correct the king's folly: so God confounds the wisdom of the world, for no nation gloried more in its universal knowledge, as Isaiah reproached them. Gill has the staff handed over and the brother going to the water side, and argues the reality of the change from the fish, since had the water only worn the colour of blood they would have lived as before; the loss touched Egypt less in drink than in food, fish being what the common people lived on.

Clarke reads the clause about vessels simply, as extending the stroke to water already carried indoors; he mentions the suggestion that the two vessels refer instead to filtering that thick water through pots of white earth, but prefers the plain sense. He insists the change was real and not in appearance only, the water becoming corrupt, so that the fish died and the smell grew offensive. Wesley, repeating the charge that the river was served above the Creator, turns it to use: every creature is to us what he makes it, water or blood; what is water today may be blood tomorrow, and what is vain may soon become vexatious — for it is sin that turns our waters into blood.

Ellicott sets out what the command covered: the main stream, its branches, the canals drawn from it, the ponds left by the inundation, and the reservoirs in gardens, courts and houses. There is no other stream in the land, and no natural springs or brooks; water can be had by digging, but the soil is impregnated with nitre and the well water unpalatable. This verse, he adds, shows a very exact knowledge of that system. The vessels of wood and stone he explains from the practice of storing river water in tanks to drop its sediment, such cisterns standing in all the better houses. He is certain the lifter of the rod is Aaron, and dwells on who watched: if the day was a festival of the river, the king would have gone out attended by the officers of the court, priests and vast numbers of people; if merely for bathing, he would still have had a train. Either way the sign was public. He marks a small advance in the wording too: before they had loathed to drink, yet apparently drank; now they could not, the draught being too nauseous.

22.pericope_label: The magicians did so; and seven days were fulfilled

schools.summary: Calvin supposes clear water appeared for a little while and was then changed, God opening a way for himself until the contests reached their end; the notion that the court's men fetched it from the dwellings of Israel he calls forced. Whether the change was true or imaginary he dare not decide, except that it accords better with satanic delusion that the eyes of the wicked were deceived, as Paul says God sends error to those who refuse the truth. On the king's indifference he fastens hard: the clause proves the hardness voluntary and the sin his own, God's secret appointment availing nothing to lessen his blame, since blinded by pride he took no account of the glory before him. So the wicked, though cast into a reprobate mind, still harden themselves, running against God willfully, and their audacity takes away the excuse of ignorance — which warns us not to slumber when God arouses us. In the digging, and more in the seven days, Calvin finds an increase of certainty: had the corruption been momentary some suspicion of trickery might have crept in, which the continued taste and appearance removed. Gill dates the plague from the eighteenth to the twenty-fifth of the sixth month, and observes that no request for its removal is recorded, though one ancient writer says otherwise; it was lifted unasked.

Clarke answers the obvious difficulty from the digging that follows: pits were sunk along the river, and that water was not bloody. He adds that though the commission covered streams and pools, only the river is said to have been smitten at first, so other water lay ready for imitation, to which juggling or a familiar spirit could give a bloody look and a fetid smell. He reads the stroke as retributive — that river had been made the grave of the Hebrew male children by the murderous decree, and now the water necessary to their own life was deadly; and since a girl, some say a boy and a girl, was yearly sacrificed to it in gratitude, the contempt poured on it tended to correct their notions. Weighing why God should contend with such men at all, he passes on four reasons: that they be let exert their utmost, lest the wonders be laid to magic; that wavering Israel might see the difference; that they be afterwards safe from false signs; and, in mercy to Egypt, that the gods they trusted be seen unable to undo one plague. Wesley notes with Gill how mean the performance was.

Ellicott makes the imitation poor beside the original: the brothers had changed river, canals, lakes and reservoirs, while the court's men could only work on some small quantity, reddening it or substituting blood by sleight of hand, with no test applied and no hostile witness — enough, though, to let the king harden himself. He is careful with the idiom of the king's indifference: he did not set his heart — pay attention — even to this, but passed it over as a slight matter and went home; care was probably taken to keep him supplied from the wells, brackish though they were, sufficient for his customary washings, while he drank a more generous liquid. On the digging he explains that wells sunk anywhere in the alluvium always yield water, brackish and unpalatable, drawn by percolation from the river, but percolation is slow and blood would scarcely travel far by it, so what they reached was probably in the ground already and never subject to the sign. He takes the week as the plague's duration, lengthened because no submission was made.
